## {#decisions-surface data-menu-title="Decisions Surface"}

[What those decisions reveal]{.slide-title}

::: {.body-text}
The decisions you're describing — threshold at 70 mm,
whether to drop NAs, stacked vs. dodged bars — are not
wrong or right.

**They are scientific choices that need to be documented.**

This is exactly what a decision log is for.

The MPA bonus question is a good example: adding
`DESIGNATION` changes what you can ask. That's a
modeling decision that belongs in your methods.
:::

## {#quarto-yaml-options data-menu-title="YAML Options"}

[Controlling your published output]{.slide-title}

::: {.body-text}
The YAML header of your `index.qmd` controls how your
page looks and behaves. A few high-value options:

```yaml
---
title: "My Research"
author: "Your Name"
date: today
toc: true
toc-depth: 2
number-sections: true
theme: cosmo
---
```

- `toc: true` — adds a clickable table of contents
- `theme:` — changes the visual appearance
- `date: today` — auto-inserts the render date
:::

---

## {#themes data-menu-title="Themes"}

[Quarto HTML themes]{.slide-title}

::: {.body-text}
Quarto ships with the Bootswatch theme library. You can
preview all of them at `bootswatch.com`.

Popular options for scientific documents:

| Theme | Character |
|---|---|
| `cosmo` | Clean, modern, readable |
| `flatly` | Minimal, professional |
| `journal` | Slightly more editorial |
| `lumen` | Light and airy |
| `sandstone` | Earthy, warm |

Change one word in your YAML and re-render.
:::

---

## {#quarto-yml data-menu-title="_quarto.yml"}

[Site-wide settings with `_quarto.yml`]{.slide-title}

::: {.body-text}
When you have multiple `.qmd` files that should all
look the same, don't repeat YAML in each file.

Create `_quarto.yml` at the root of your project:

```yaml
project:
  type: website

website:
  title: "My Research Project"
  navbar:
    left:
      - href: index.qmd
        text: Home
      - href: analysis/data-cleaning.qmd
        text: Data Cleaning

format:
  html:
    theme: cosmo
    toc: true
```

Now all pages share the same settings.
:::

---

## {#what-quarto-yml-enables data-menu-title="What _quarto.yml Enables"}

[What a `_quarto.yml` unlocks]{.slide-title}

::: {.body-text}
With `_quarto.yml` and `type: website`, your repo
becomes a proper multi-page site:

- Consistent navigation bar across all pages
- Shared theme, font, and layout
- `quarto render` builds every page at once
- `quarto preview` lets you see the full site locally

**You don't need this for today's activity** — a single
`index.qmd` with links is enough.

But for a thesis project site, this is how it's done.
:::

---

## {#thesis-connection data-menu-title="Thesis Connection"}

[Connecting this to your thesis]{.slide-title}

::: {.body-text}
Imagine your thesis project as a GitHub Pages site:

```
index.qmd          ← Project overview and data description
analysis/
  01-clean.qmd     ← Data cleaning and decisions
  02-explore.qmd   ← Exploratory analysis
  03-model.qmd     ← Statistical modeling
  04-figures.qmd   ← Publication figures

data/              ← Raw data (or link to repository)
figs/              ← Saved figure outputs
```

Your committee sees a URL. Your advisor can open it
without installing R. Your methods are reproducible.
:::

---

## {#sharing-work data-menu-title="Sharing Work"}

[Who is your audience?]{.slide-title}

::: {.body-text}
Different audiences need different things from your site.

**Advisor:** can they trace your logic from raw data
to conclusion? Is the decision log visible?

**Collaborator who doesn't use R:** can they see the
visualizations and read your interpretations without
running anything?

**Future you:** can you pick this up in six months
and understand what you did and why?

**The site forces you to write for all three.**
:::

---

## {#open-science data-menu-title="Open Science"}

[Open science in practice]{.slide-title}

::: {.body-text}
Many journals now request or require:

- Data availability statements
- Analysis code shared openly
- Reproducible workflows

A GitHub Pages site with your Quarto analyses satisfies
all three.

Some journals will link directly to your GitHub repo
or your published site in the supplementary materials.

**You're not just learning a tool. You're building
a practice.**
:::

## {#common-issues data-menu-title="Common Issues"}

[Troubleshooting GitHub Pages]{.slide-title}

::: {.body-text}
**Site shows "404" or won't load:**

- Is `index.html` committed *and* pushed?
- Did you activate Pages in Settings → Pages → main → root?
- Wait 2 minutes and hard refresh

**Link goes to a `.qmd` instead of `.html`:**

- Your link must point to the rendered `.html` file
- Render the file first, then commit the `.html`

**Old content showing:**

- GitHub sometimes caches aggressively
- Try the URL in a private/incognito window
:::

## {#sf-teaser data-menu-title="sf Teaser"}

[From coordinates to geometry]{.slide-title}

::: {.body-text}
Right now you know how to plot points on a map
using latitude and longitude columns in a data frame.

`sf` objects go further:

```r
library(sf)

# A data frame becomes spatial
lobster_sf <- st_as_sf(lobster_data,
                       coords = c("longitude", "latitude"),
                       crs = 4326)

# Now you can do spatial joins, buffering, and more
```

The coordinate reference system (CRS) is what makes
"spatial" different from "just columns with numbers."
:::
